options.name: Prioritize the Advanced Supplemental Payment
options.who_is_affected: City budget bears additional supplemental pension contributions above the statutory ramp; pension systems and future taxpayers benefit from reduced unfunded liability and more predictable future required contributions.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility High (depends on fiscal capacity) / Timing Long. Does not generate near-term budgetary relief; a timing-based funding mechanism, not a short-term cost-savings tool.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.30) argues the slate should also address the pension liability itself, not just the contribution side — e.g., recommending the Illinois Constitution be amended so non-vested pension liabilities could be revised prospectively. Accelerating contributions would require additional taxes in an already high-tax environment, and in the absence of corresponding liability reform may not achieve the intended result. (Argues the recommendation is one-sided/incomplete, not that it goes too far.)
options.verbatim_anchor: make the advanced supplemental payment each year until the calculation is no longer necessary

options.name: Secure Chicago Public Schools (CPS) Contributions to City Pensions
options.who_is_affected: CPS would contribute the full portion of its non-teacher employees' pensions into the Municipal (MEABF) fund; the City's Corporate Fund is relieved of part of that burden. Models an agreement (potentially through the State) to provide funding.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Low-Medium (requires agreement with CPS/State) / Timing Long. Report states a goal of CPS paying $175 million per year for the first 10 years. Past funding came via Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA); ability to obtain funding the same way is likely limited going forward.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.31) notes the City/CPS/State relationship is complex and additional analysis may be needed given CPS's own financial and educational funding needs and the State's broader responsibility for teachers outside CPS. The City has had limited practical ability to direct CPS to pay, a dynamic that shifts further with a fully elected school board; the recommendation may be most effective if focused on State legislation governing the City's MEABF deposit, possibly paired with the State moving CPS teachers into TRS or covering the full CTPF contribution.
options.verbatim_anchor: paying $175 million per year for the first 10 years

options.name: Offer Voluntary Buy-Outs
options.who_is_affected: Retirees/participants could choose a reduced-value lump sum instead of monthly pension checks; the City reduces long-term liabilities in exchange for upfront cash outlays. Outcomes depend on individual decisions.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Low-Medium / Feasibility Medium (program creation feasible) / Timing Medium. A supplementary tool, not a primary strategy; impact limited because participation is voluntary.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.32) argues the recommendation appears to produce no net benefit to the pension plans because the buyout would be calculated at an NPV neutral to the plan. While attractive to individual pensioners, the Task Force's focus is the City's liabilities and this may not meaningfully advance that objective; widespread adoption could also have the unintended effect of accelerating withdrawals and straining plan assets over time.
options.verbatim_anchor: Allow retirees to choose a lump-sum payout instead of monthly checks

options.name: Dedicate External Funding to Pay Actuarially Determined Contribution (ADC)
options.who_is_affected: Outside funding sources (state, federal, gaming, asset deals, e.g. a potential 'millionaire' tax) would be routed to pension funding targeting 100% funding over a fixed period, relieving pressure on the City's operating budget; pension systems benefit.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Low / Timing Long. Effectiveness depends on the scale and reliability of external funding sources.
options.dissent_summary: Two dissents. Dissent A (p.32) argues paying the ADC would require the City to target 100% funding rather than the 90% required by State law, increasing costs today for the benefit of taxpayers in 2056 and 2058; while actuaries generally support 100% funding, many government finance experts and bond rating agencies consider 80%-90% appropriate (i.e., the option may go too far). Dissent B (p.33) suggests the more appropriate direction may be to evaluate whether the funding percentage target on the pension ramp could be lowered.
options.verbatim_anchor: Bring in money from outside sources (state, federal, gaming, asset deals)

options.name: Require State Fiscal Note for New Pension Legislation
options.who_is_affected: State legislative process: any State proposal to alter pension benefits, contributions, or funding policy would require a standardized fiscal note; improves transparency for the City and public. No reduction to current liabilities.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility High / Timing Short (immediate once enacted); modest political risk. A supermajority vote would be required to exempt any proposal.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.33) argues the City already has the authority to estimate the fiscal impact of proposed laws and communicate its views to the General Assembly; these existing tools may be both more practical and more effective than seeking new legislation governing the General Assembly's internal procedures.
options.verbatim_anchor: must include a standardized fiscal note

options.name: Require State-Dedicated Funding for Any State Actions Increasing City Pension Costs
options.who_is_affected: Any future State action increasing City pension liabilities/contributions would have to be paired with a dedicated State-funded revenue stream earmarked for pension improvements; prevents recurrence of unfunded benefit increases.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility Low (State action required) / Timing Long. A supermajority vote would be required to exempt any proposal.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.34) warns of unintended consequences: a new state statute requiring dedicated revenue could result in existing revenue sources being committed for a particular purpose, effectively giving the General Assembly a role in shaping the City's budget and limiting the City's ability to set its own priorities (in tension with revenue-raising flexibility sought elsewhere). Notes the recommendation envisions a new dedicated stream rather than dedicating an existing one, and that the timeline/complexity of state-level action is worth acknowledging.
options.verbatim_anchor: must include a dedicated State-funded revenue stream to be earmarked for pension improvements

options.name: Consolidate Fund Actuaries or Administrators
options.who_is_affected: Chicago's four pension systems would share actuarial/administrative providers and/or state oversight; improves consistency and oversight and creates operational efficiencies without altering benefit structures.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Low-Medium / Feasibility Medium (operational consolidation) / Timing Medium. Covers actuarial services procurement, experience studies/assumption governance, shared admin/investment operations, centralized reporting.
options.verbatim_anchor: Consolidate actuarial or administrative providers across the funds and/or with state oversight

options.name: Establish Formal, Routine Interactions Between City and State Officials for Pension-Specific Matters
options.who_is_affected: City finance leadership, pension fund leadership, and State officials would coordinate pension-related topics through a formal intergovernmental mechanism; improves alignment on funding policy, legislative changes, and long-term planning.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility High (administrative coordination) / Timing Short (immediate). Group should meet at least twice per year with a sustainable routine check-in format.
options.verbatim_anchor: Create a formal intergovernmental mechanism (liaison/working group/standing committee)

options.name: Strengthen Claims, Litigation, and Compliance Management
options.who_is_affected: City reduces settlement/judgment costs (often legacy police-related incidents) and consent-decree compliance costs; affects Law Department, outside counsel, City departments, and parties to tort claims. Within City control.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium-High (within City control) / Timing Medium. Recommendations: review legacy/current claims for alternative litigation strategies; consolidate outside counsel firms; track infrastructure-related tort claims to prioritize repairs; fill restored Chicago Police Department consent-decree positions and accelerate early-warning systems to deescalate compliance deficiencies.
options.verbatim_anchor: control costs related to the City's tort settlements and judgments

options.name: Inventory and Monetize Non-Core Assets with Oversight
options.who_is_affected: City would generate new revenue from real estate, infrastructure, and public space (including digital/outdoor advertising and infrastructure partnerships) under centralized governance and oversight; affects City residents/public spaces.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility Medium (requires inventory and governance) / Timing Medium. Recommendations: engage a professional firm to inventory monetizable assets; join GFOA's Public Asset Wealth Strategy program; conduct a feasibility study on advertising; establish an Asset Optimization Oversight Committee (incl. two City Council members, OBM, Fleet & Facility Management, Law, Inspector General, Planning & Development). Findings must conform to the cultural and historical nature of the City.
options.verbatim_anchor: explore the potential monetization of eligible City assets

options.name: Benchmark Taxes, Fees, and Expenditures Continuously
options.who_is_affected: City residents and businesses bearing taxes/fees/fines; the City uses peer benchmarking to decide where to raise or lower revenue and where to find efficiencies. Report states certain taxes/fees/fines will need to remain elevated until pension underfunding is corrected.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires analytical continuity) / Timing Long. Cautions the City cannot solely tax its way out of structural deficits; must also reduce expenditures and increase efficiency.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.47) argues the City should fully explore the range of taxing options available for higher-income individuals and large businesses alongside any consideration of increases to taxes, fees, and fines that impact low- and middle-income households, regardless of how those rates compare to peer cities. (Argues for a more progressive approach.)
options.verbatim_anchor: Continue to assess where it stands relative to comparable cities regarding taxes/fees/fines

options.name: Establish City-County Governance Alignment & Functional Consolidation
options.who_is_affected: Chicago and Cook County, which run parallel departments in overlapping functions; consolidation/realignment would reduce duplication in administrative systems, staffing, and service delivery and improve accountability.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires intergovernmental alignment) / Timing Long (multi-year). Recommends a joint Governance Alignment Commission with Cook County; initial priority to evaluate consolidating election administration under a single countywide entity; may require statutory changes, IGAs, or voter referenda.
options.verbatim_anchor: Jointly establish with Cook County a formal Governance Alignment Commission

options.name: Pursue Graduated Income Tax Authorization (State Constitutional Amendment)
options.who_is_affected: Higher-income filers (income above $1 million) under a graduated rate structure; corporations (paired changes maintaining the 8-to-5 corporate-to-personal ratio); could reduce reliance on local revenues that constrain economic growth. Alternative: raise the flat income tax rate with a refundable credit shielding middle/lower-income filers.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Low (requires State constitutional change) / Timing Long. Specific rates to be set pending an impact study. Passing a constitutional amendment could take years.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.48-49) argues any change to tax structure/rates should be considered in the broader context of the State's and City's structural fiscal issues and economic growth; higher taxes and the messaging around them may affect perceptions of the business climate as regions compete for talent and investment, so proposals merit careful evaluation and a detailed long-term plan. Also raises concerns about the refundable tax credit alternative: possible constitutional challenges, the reality that all taxpayers would pay the higher rate before a refund, and that a similar amendment was previously put on the ballot and did not pass. (Cautionary — option may go too far / risk growth.)
options.verbatim_anchor: enabling legislation allowing a proposal on the ballot ... graduated rate structure

options.name: Restructure Electricity Tax Rates
options.who_is_affected: Current inverse rate design has smaller users (residential households, small businesses) paying higher marginal rates and larger users lower rates; restructuring would raise rates on higher-volume users while holding residential and small business customers harmless, expanding the City's effective taxable base.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (State action required to change the statutory rate structure) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.49) argues it is important to consider how the change could impact the City's business climate; before pursuing a change there should be comprehensive analysis showing how the potential new rate structure compares to other jurisdictions. (Cautionary.)
options.verbatim_anchor: changes the statutorily required inverse rate structure on electricity tax

options.name: Fully Staff Tax Auditor Positions and Streamline Revenue-Generating Hiring
options.who_is_affected: Direct revenue generation through enforcement collections; affects taxpayers subject to audit. City's Department of Finance Tax Division staffing.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (hiring and retention required) / Timing Medium. DOF data: individual City auditors have historically generated approximately $1.0 million to $4.5 million in annual enforcement collections since 2016, averaging around $3 million per auditor. A fully staffed Tax Division is anticipated to generate up to $56 million in additional annual collections (the captured dollar_estimate is this 'up to $56 million' figure).
options.verbatim_anchor: fully staffed Tax Division anticipated to generate up to $56 million in additional annual collections

options.name: Mandate Intergovernmental Data Sharing to Enhance Debt Collection Efficiency
options.who_is_affected: City improves collection of its ~$8.5 billion in outstanding receivables (unpaid fees, fines, judgments) via mandatory data-sharing with State/County agencies (Illinois Secretary of State, Cook County Clerk's Office, Cook County Treasurer); affects debtors and delinquent property owners.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires agreements across agencies) / Timing Medium. The ~$8.5 billion is a stated receivables balance (context), not a savings estimate. Automated CCCO and Cook County Treasurer data feeds would speed lien/foreclosure identification and cross-referencing.
options.verbatim_anchor: pursuing mandatory data-sharing agreements with State and County agencies

options.name: Pursue Legislative Amendments to Strengthen Vehicle Violation Debt Enforcement
options.who_is_affected: Targets one of the largest, fastest-growing categories of outstanding City debt; affects holders of vehicle-violation debt. Improves enforceability of collections.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (legislative dependency) / Timing Long. Two targeted amendments: (1) amend 625 ILCS 5/11-208.3(f) to allow registering a transcript of a final determination and pursuing it as a court judgment; (2) amend 735 ILCS 5/13-227 to allow more time to convert a violation into a formal judgment enforceable over a longer period.
options.verbatim_anchor: amendments to Illinois state law to strengthen the City's ability to collect vehicle violation debts

options.name: Strengthen Compliance with Outstanding City Fees, Fines and Other Obligations Across Public Employees and Agencies
options.who_is_affected: City employees and sister agencies who owe outstanding City debt; focuses on improving compliance within the public sector rather than external enforcement against the general public.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (operational reform required) / Timing Medium. Recommends IGAs requiring pre-employment debt checks against selected candidates at sister agencies, mandating extinguishment of outstanding City debt as a condition of employment, building on existing quarterly notifications and wage garnishment.
options.verbatim_anchor: improve collection of outstanding fees and fines owed by the City's sister agencies

options.name: Conduct Total Cost of Ownership Assessment Across IT Footprint
options.who_is_affected: City departments with distributed technology investments; a consolidated 'total cost of ownership' view establishes a baseline for modernization decisions and helps capture system-wide efficiencies.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility High (straightforward analysis) / Timing Short (immediate). Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed to accelerate technology purchases.
options.verbatim_anchor: citywide "total cost of ownership" assessment across infrastructure, applications, security

options.name: Perform Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
options.who_is_affected: Reduces fiscal risk exposure from data breaches, downtime, and recovery costs; protects resident and employee data; affects City departments running legacy/unsupported systems.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility High (readily executable) / Timing Short (near-term). Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: citywide cybersecurity risk and readiness assessment focused on fiscal sustainability

options.name: Standardize Enterprise Platforms
options.who_is_affected: City departments using separate agency-specific systems; transitioning to a shared, scalable enterprise platform reduces duplicative costs and ongoing maintenance and enables shared-services models.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility Medium (cross-agency coordination required) / Timing Medium. Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: Transition from agency-specific solutions to a secure, scalable enterprise platform

options.name: Upskill Workforce for AI and Automation
options.who_is_affected: City employees, who would be trained to leverage cloud platforms, AI, and low-code/no-code automation; enables efficiency gains from technology adoption.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires training programs) / Timing Medium. Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: Invest in workforce upskilling so employees can leverage modern tools

options.name: Deploy Targeted AI Use Cases for Administrative Functions
options.who_is_affected: High-volume administrative functions and the residents they serve; automation/AI streamlines backlogged or burdensome processes (AI-assisted police report drafting, automated tax auditing, back-office ERP automation, improved 311 operations).
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires integration + governance) / Timing Long (multi-year). Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: Deploy AI for targeted use cases that are backlogged or administratively burdensome

options.name: Establish AI Governance Framework
options.who_is_affected: City functions adopting AI tools; a citywide governance policy mitigates risk related to accuracy, bias, transparency, oversight, and public trust.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (policy + governance effort) / Timing Long (multi-year). Policy to include transparency best practices, workforce training, bias/hallucination checks, and a review process. Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: clear governance systems, procedures, human oversight, and evaluation processes for AI systems

options.name: Implement Workforce Transition Strategy to Support IT Modernization
options.who_is_affected: City workers affected by technology-enabled change; a 'just transition' (retraining, upskilling, redeployment) preserves workforce stability and institutional knowledge. Requires coordination/negotiation with labor unions.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires coordination with labor) / Timing Long (multi-year). Recommends use of IT infrastructure bonds as needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: paired with a just transition for workers, focused on retraining, upskilling, and redeployment

options.name: Consolidate CPL Management Reporting
options.who_is_affected: Chicago Public Library (CPL) and City leadership; a single consolidated financial view (CPL-managed and city-managed, Library Fund and other Funds) enables visibility into the structural gap and informed funding-shortfall decisions.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (data consolidation needed) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissent (p.57) applying to all library recommendations (16-20): the library recommendations are more operational than others in the slate, and it may be worth asking why this level of operational detail applies to libraries but not other departments, given the library system's relatively small share of the City budget and multiple funding mechanisms. Without quantifiable fiscal projections, cost-savings analyses, savings targets, or revenue implications it is difficult to assess financial impact relative to the structural deficit; the dissent also notes CPL should not be treated solely as a cost center given documented economic returns, and that this guidance may be better handled through a separate operational review.
options.verbatim_anchor: Build a single, consolidated view of CPL revenues and expenses

options.name: Develop CPL Systemwide Strategic Plan
options.who_is_affected: CPL system and the branches/neighborhoods it serves; a system-level strategic plan sets systemwide priorities, identifies acceptable tradeoffs, and explains differences in resource allocation across branches given the Library Fund projected deficit.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (leadership-driven) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissent (p.57) applying to all library recommendations (16-20): library recs are more operational than other slate items; questions applying this operational detail to libraries given their small budget share and multiple funding sources; lacks fiscal projections/savings targets to assess impact on the structural deficit; CPL shouldn't be treated solely as a cost center; may be better addressed via a separate operational review.
options.verbatim_anchor: Develop a system-level strategic plan that sets clear systemwide priorities

options.name: Define CPL Branch Service Priorities
options.who_is_affected: CPL branches and neighborhoods; defining specific service goals per neighborhood/branch (access, engagement, demand, basic coverage) guides where limited dollars are concentrated or held steady.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (operational redesign) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissent (p.57) applying to all library recommendations (16-20): library recs are more operational than other slate items; questions applying this operational detail to libraries given their small budget share and multiple funding sources; lacks fiscal projections/savings targets to assess impact on the structural deficit; CPL shouldn't be treated solely as a cost center; may be better addressed via a separate operational review.
options.verbatim_anchor: Define specific service goals for each neighborhood and branch

options.name: Tailor CPL Services by Neighborhood
options.who_is_affected: CPL branches and neighborhoods; tailoring staffing, programming, hours, and delivery formats to community conditions and usage patterns improves outcomes without new spend, within what the Library Fund can sustain.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (requires service redesign) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissent (p.57) applying to all library recommendations (16-20): library recs are more operational than other slate items; questions applying this operational detail to libraries given their small budget share and multiple funding sources; lacks fiscal projections/savings targets to assess impact on the structural deficit; CPL shouldn't be treated solely as a cost center; may be better addressed via a separate operational review.
options.verbatim_anchor: Tailor service models to each neighborhood's needs and what the library fund can sustain

options.name: Analyze and Scale CPL Branch Best Practices
options.who_is_affected: CPL system; studying performance differences across branches identifies cost-effective practices to scale system-wide without additional funding, emphasizing how services are delivered rather than how much is spent.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (data-driven approach) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissent (p.57) applying to all library recommendations (16-20): library recs are more operational than other slate items; questions applying this operational detail to libraries given their small budget share and multiple funding sources; lacks fiscal projections/savings targets to assess impact on the structural deficit; CPL shouldn't be treated solely as a cost center; may be better addressed via a separate operational review. (This dissent block immediately follows recommendation 20.)
options.verbatim_anchor: Study differences across branches to find cost-effective practices

options.name: Limit Personal Property Replacement Tax (PPRT) Diversions
options.who_is_affected: Restores state-shared PPRT revenue to municipalities (including Chicago) by limiting State diversions; also proposes leveling S-Corporation/trust/partnership tax rates with C-Corporation rates. Affects the State and businesses.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (state action required) / Timing Long.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissents (p.60) applying to the 'Additional Fees, Fines, and Taxes' recommendations (21-25). Dissent A: additional taxing authority from Springfield could enable progressive options (payroll tax, delivery tax, taxing income/occupations). Dissent B: the City should also engage in cost-benefit analyses for these recommendations. Dissent C primarily concerns recs 23 and 24 (CPI property tax and sales-tax expansion).
options.verbatim_anchor: limit PPRT revenue diversions only to what is necessary to administer and distribute

options.name: Increase the Local Government Distributive Fund (LGDF) Share Rate
options.who_is_affected: Municipalities (including Chicago) receiving a share of State income tax revenue; reverting LGDF to the pre-2011 10% share (from ~6.5% currently) restores a more stable, scalable revenue source. Affects the State. (Also included in the Interim Report.)
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (state-dependent) / Timing Long. Major recurring revenue upside; the 10% vs ~6.5% figures are stated rate percentages, not a dollar estimate.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissents (p.60) applying to the 'Additional Fees, Fines, and Taxes' recommendations (21-25). Dissent A: Springfield could grant authority for progressive options (payroll/delivery tax, taxing income/occupations). Dissent B: City should engage in cost-benefit analyses. Dissent C primarily concerns recs 23 and 24.
options.verbatim_anchor: 2011 percentage share of state income tax revenue distributed from LGDF

options.name: Resume Consumer Price Index-Based (CPI) Property Tax Increases
options.who_is_affected: Property taxpayers; resuming annual CPI-indexed adjustments to the property tax levy keeps revenue aligned with inflation (many expenditures grow with inflation). Within City policy control. (Also included in the Interim Report.)
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (within policy control) / Timing Long (ongoing).
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissents (p.60) applying to recs 21-25. Dissent C specifically: indexing real estate taxes to CPI raises concerns — if housing prices rise with inflation real estate taxes naturally rise, but requiring homeowners to pay increasingly higher real estate taxes during periods when property values are stagnant or declining presents a meaningful concern, meriting further analysis. (Cautionary — may go too far in some conditions.) Dissent A also urges exploring progressive options; Dissent B urges cost-benefit analysis.
options.verbatim_anchor: Consider resuming annual adjustments to its property tax levy by CPI

options.name: Expand the Sales Tax Base to Include Consumer Services
options.who_is_affected: Consumers of services; expanding the sales tax to broadly encompass consumer services (excluding healthcare, business-to-business, and professional services) modernizes the tax base. Affects the State (requires State legislation). (Also included in the Interim Report.)
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (state legislation required) / Timing Long. After State adoption, the City would review existing consumption-based taxes to ensure economic growth.
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissents (p.60) applying to recs 21-25. Dissent C specifically: expanding sales taxes to consumer services raises questions meriting further analysis — given sales tax rates in the City are already high, further expansion should be carefully evaluated. (Cautionary.) Dissent A urges exploring progressive options; Dissent B urges cost-benefit analysis.
options.verbatim_anchor: expand the sales tax to broadly encompass all consumer services

options.name: Implement Cordon Model Congestion Pricing
options.who_is_affected: Vehicles entering or exiting the central area during weekday rush hours pay a fixed fee; generates recurring revenue and reduces congestion. An equity-based design (exemptions, discounts, transit investment) would reduce disproportionate impacts on lower-income residents or those with limited transportation options.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (operational & political complexity) / Timing Long (multi-year).
options.dissent_summary: Shared dissents (p.60) applying to the 'Additional Fees, Fines, and Taxes' recommendations (21-25). Dissent A: Springfield could grant authority for progressive options such as a payroll tax or delivery tax. Dissent B: the City should engage in cost-benefit analyses. (Dissent C is specific to recs 23 and 24.)
options.verbatim_anchor: equity-based cordon-model congestion pricing ... subject to a fixed fee

options.name: Convene a Mayor's Business Council for Corporate Engagement
options.who_is_affected: Chicago's top 30 employers (by employment or tax contribution, incl. corporate HQs, healthcare systems, universities, anchor institutions) and the City; a proactive retention/growth platform surfaces business retention risks and workforce needs earlier. ~375,000 jobs among the top 30 employers; preventing even a 1% contraction would preserve ~3,750 jobs.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility High (can be established via Mayor + WBC coordination without new legislation) / Timing Short-Medium. Illustrative jobs figures are context, not a dollar estimate.
options.verbatim_anchor: create a formal Mayor's Business Council composed of Chicago's top 30 employers

options.name: Reinvest in and Operate a Priority Corridor Business Support Program
options.who_is_affected: Neighborhood commercial corridors (particularly South and West sides), local businesses, and community-based organizations serving as corridor managers; drives neighborhood business density and corridor activity tied to local tax generation. Builds on INVEST South/West and existing City/community infrastructure.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium-High (builds on prior corridor program) / Timing Medium. Illustrative benchmarks: priority corridor areas average ~23 households per local business vs ~13 citywide; ~700 net new businesses could support an estimated 10,000-15,000 direct/indirect jobs; Main Street America estimates every $1 invested generates roughly $18 in new public and private investment.
options.verbatim_anchor: Renew the priority corridor management program

options.name: Establish Soft, Fast Landing Program for International Companies
options.who_is_affected: Foreign companies establishing their first U.S./Chicagoland presence; a non-financial concierge-style support model (co-working/incubator space, legal/accounting/immigration connections, market-entry guidance) improves FDI conversion. Delivered with WBC and incubator operators.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (can launch with WBC/incubator partners) / Timing Short-Medium. Context: City FDI capital expenditures declined from over $1 billion/year average (2014-2021) to $674 million in 2025; 2025 FDI projects down to 26 from an average of 40+; 346 foreign-headquartered companies maintain secondary office presence. Dedicated concierge contact for each company's first 12-18 months.
options.verbatim_anchor: Soft, Fast Landing Program that provides foreign companies with turnkey support

options.name: Deploy Capital Recruitment Strategy
options.who_is_affected: Outside and local investors; a curated project prospectus and coordinated investor-conference strategy converts interest into deployable capital, supporting construction, jobs, and long-term tax base growth. In tandem with WBC and an Office of Marketing & Promotion.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility Medium (requires coordinated prospectus and investor outreach) / Timing Medium-Long. Context: at least $185 billion deployed into Chicago-based companies in 2025; a 2% increase could represent billions in additional deployed capital; even $1 billion incremental annual investment could generate substantial construction, jobs, and fiscal benefits (illustrative, not a stated estimate).
options.verbatim_anchor: Develop a capital attraction strategy for major projects and developments

options.name: Open International "Offices" to Attract Foreign Business Capital to the City
options.who_is_affected: Foreign businesses and investors; a dedicated in-market presence (representative offices or contracted market leads in priority markets) sustains relationships that drive FDI. Benchmarked to London, Singapore, Texas, Georgia models. In tandem with international delegations and consular engagement.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Low-Medium (requires sustained overseas presence and recurring funding) / Timing Long (3+ years).
options.verbatim_anchor: Establish a dedicated presence in key international markets to act as a liaison

options.name: Expand Local Purchasing Commitments
options.who_is_affected: Chicago-based small businesses and minority business enterprises (MBEs), anchor institutions and major employers (hospitals, universities, cultural institutions); directing more procurement spend locally retains revenue in neighborhood business corridors. Benchmarked to Cleveland, Philadelphia, NYC.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires coordination with anchors/employers and tracking) / Timing Medium. Illustrative: shifting just 1% of institutional purchasing toward Chicago-based businesses could support thousands of jobs. Proposes a phased 'ChicagoMade' brand and recognition strategy.
options.verbatim_anchor: Optimize and expand local purchasing commitments across the City of Chicago

options.name: Relaunch the Chicago Supplier Development Program
options.who_is_affected: Minority-owned and qualified local suppliers navigating public and private procurement; relaunching the BACP Supplier Development Program builds readiness and pipelines into corporate purchasing. Benchmarked to Chicago MSDC and peer-city supplier diversity efforts.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (feasible through BACP and partner organizations) / Timing Medium. Illustrative: if 250 firms annually secured an additional $500,000 in private-sector contracts, this would represent approximately $125 million in new local business revenue (illustrative scenario, not a stated estimate).
options.verbatim_anchor: Relaunch the inactive ... Chicago Supplier Development Program

options.name: Expand Industry-Focused Innovation Hubs
options.who_is_affected: Startups in targeted industries (physical product, advanced manufacturing, industrial technology) and the entrepreneurial ecosystem; building from models like mHUB provides shared prototyping labs, accelerators, and industry connections. Benchmarked to Boston, Pittsburgh, Toronto.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires sustained funding and ecosystem coordination) / Timing Long. Illustrative mHUB track record: 500+ startups supported, ~$2.0 billion in revenue generated, $2.5 billion in capital attracted, 7,200+ jobs created since 2017 (illustrative model outcomes). Audit against Chicago's BUILDS framework.
options.verbatim_anchor: launch new or further support existing innovation and convening hubs for key growth industries

options.name: Designate Strategic Industry Districts
options.who_is_affected: Firms, institutions, and enabling infrastructure within defined districts; coordinated district designation (with zoning, public realm, and incentive alignment via TIFs, BIDs, infrastructure support) reinforces competitive advantages. Benchmarked to Boston Seaport, Houston Energy Corridor, Brooklyn Navy Yard.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Low-Medium (requires alignment of zoning, incentives, infrastructure) / Timing Long. Illustrative peer outcomes: Houston's Energy Corridor supports 64,000+ jobs and ~$15 billion economic impact; Brooklyn Navy Yard contributes $2.5 billion+ annually (illustrative, not stated estimates).
options.verbatim_anchor: designate and market new industry districts to better align business attraction, marketing, and incentives

options.name: Support Workforce Development Hub for the Future of Work
options.who_is_affected: Employers, educators, workers, and workforce systems; a centralized 'future of work' hub aligns evolving skill needs in growth sectors (quantum, life sciences, advanced manufacturing, clean energy) and identifies occupations at risk from automation. Benchmarked to NYC, Atlanta, Indianapolis, London roadmaps.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires coordination across employers and education institutions) / Timing Medium-Long. Illustrative: closing even part of the postings-to-hires mismatch could fill tens of thousands of positions annually.
options.verbatim_anchor: Support the development of a Workforce Development Hub

options.name: Create Readiness Programs for City-Supported Development and Procurement
options.who_is_affected: Emerging developers, small/medium enterprises, contractors, and community organizations working with the City; structured training plus hands-on technical assistance reduces stalled projects and accelerates deployment of public dollars. Benchmarked to Detroit's Motor City Match.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (can be launched through partners and technical assistance providers) / Timing Medium. Illustrative: a 5%-10% improvement in execution rates could accelerate tens of millions in private investment. Partner with educational institutions, including exposing youth to employment opportunities.
options.verbatim_anchor: develop additional, ongoing support for key groups doing business with or supported by the City

options.name: Expand and Implement Cut the Tape Reforms
options.who_is_affected: Developers, small businesses, and housing producers facing permitting/licensing/zoning/approval friction; a second phase of Cut the Tape shortens timelines and expands by-right pathways. Builds on Mayor Brandon Johnson's Executive Order 2023-21 (Dec 2023) across 14 City departments.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium-High (builds on an existing initiative already demonstrating results) / Timing Short-Medium. Cited local results: Plan Commission review time reduced from 131 to 79 days; 1,000+ vacant properties moved toward reuse. Potential actions: automatic permit approvals for qualifying projects; by-right small multifamily in single-family and two-flat zoned parcels.
options.verbatim_anchor: Continue and expand the Cut the Tape initiative through a second phase

options.name: Expand Production of Missing Middle Infill Housing Program and Market-Rate Housing
options.who_is_affected: Middle-income households, developers, and disinvested South/West Side neighborhoods; the DPD-led Missing Middle Infill Housing Initiative sells clusters of City-owned lots to qualified developers for $1 per parcel and provides construction assistance (generally up to $150,000 per unit) from the Housing and Economic Development bond, for market-rate sale to owner-occupants. Also expands downtown office-to-residential conversions (LaSalle Street Reimagined).
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Medium (uses existing programs but depends on development pipeline) / Timing Long. Program has delivered 300+ units; $1/parcel and up-to-$150,000/unit are stated program parameters (not a savings/revenue estimate for the option).
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p.77): units receiving city subsidies should include affordability requirements as a condition of that subsidy. (Argues the option does not go far enough on affordability.)
options.verbatim_anchor: Expand the funding and rollout of the Missing Middle Infill Housing program

options.name: Activate Underutilized Downtown Real Estate Through Reuse and Programming
options.who_is_affected: Downtown office/retail property, residents, and the City's assessed tax base; pairing office-to-residential conversions with ground-floor activation, cultural programming, and streetscape investment accelerates mixed-use recovery (LaSalle Street, South State Street). Benchmarked to Calgary's conversion incentive program.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium-High / Feasibility Medium (requires coordination of incentives, zoning, private investment) / Timing Long (3+ year real estate cycles).
options.verbatim_anchor: catalyze opportunities for office-to-residential conversions, ground floor retail activation

options.name: Advance Proactive Rezoning of Opportunity Areas
options.who_is_affected: Builders, communities, and transit-served corridors; expanding by-right multifamily capacity grows housing supply where infrastructure exists and improves predictability, generating one-time construction activity and recurring local tax revenue (property, sales, utility). Benchmarked to Austin HOME, Minneapolis, Denver TOD.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (within City authority but politically sensitive) / Timing Medium-Long. DPD recommends rezoning of opportunity areas; simplifying zoning along major arterials to promote transit-oriented development without case-by-case City Council approvals.
options.verbatim_anchor: proactively identify additional opportunity areas for rezoning to allow more by-right multi-family housing

options.name: Facilitate Redevelopment of Vacant City Lots
options.who_is_affected: Neighborhoods with vacant parcels, developers, and the City; accelerating disposition and reuse of City-owned vacant land (via ChiBlockBuilder and the Missing Middle Housing program) converts underutilized assets into productive uses generating recurring revenue and property value. Benchmarked to Baltimore, Indianapolis, Houston, Philadelphia.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires coordination across agencies and disposition processes) / Timing Long (3+ years). Continue reducing the inventory of roughly 7,000 vacant parcels; map privately-owned vacant/underutilized land. Illustrative: large-scale activation could generate tens of millions in recurring annual revenue.
options.verbatim_anchor: facilitate the private purchase and redevelopment of vacant City-owned lots

options.name: Advance Transit System Enhancements and Asset Upgrades
options.who_is_affected: Residents (a top public priority for reliable, frequent transit connecting people to jobs), corridors, and the workforce; new transit opportunities (Western Avenue Bus Rapid Transit, a high-speed rail hub, improved O'Hare service) support economic and corridor development and congestion relief. Coordinated with CTA and NITA leadership.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Low-Medium (requires major capital investment and interagency coordination) / Timing Long (planning and construction exceed 3 years). Benchmarked to Cleveland HealthLine, Kansas City streetcar, Denver FasTracks.
options.verbatim_anchor: Evaluate and support new transit opportunities ... Western Avenue Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)

options.name: Create an Office of Marketing & Promotion
options.who_is_affected: City's marketing/business-attraction capacity (currently fragmented); a dedicated, self-funding Office of Marketing & Promotion consolidates promotion, integrates visitor-to-resident pathways, and develops revenue tied to brand value capture and infrastructure-based advertising. In tandem with Choose Chicago and WBC. Benchmarked to London & Partners, JobsOhio.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (requires new organizational structure and funding model) / Timing Medium.
options.verbatim_anchor: Create an Office of Marketing & Promotion

options.name: Consider a Chief Marketing Officer (CMO)
options.who_is_affected: City agencies and partner organizations with distributed marketing/communications; a centralized CMO function aligns strategy, improves ROI on existing spend, and coordinates a unified Chicago narrative. In partnership with an Office of Marketing & Promotion. Benchmarked to Los Angeles, Boston, NYC.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Low-Medium / Feasibility High (simple organizational addition) / Timing Short. Illustrative: a 5%-10% improvement in coordination could redirect millions annually toward higher-performing campaigns.
options.verbatim_anchor: Consider a CMO, in partnership with an Office of Marketing & Promotion

options.name: Launch a Citywide Data Hub
options.who_is_affected: Site selectors, investors, retailers, and companies evaluating expansion; packaging the City's aggregated municipal data into products (premium subscription/licensing) creates a recurring non-tax revenue stream while reducing barriers to market entry. Benchmarked to NYC Open Data, LA GeoHub, Singapore.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Low-Medium (new revenue stream of uncertain scale) / Feasibility Medium-High (requires data aggregation and governance) / Timing Medium.
options.verbatim_anchor: Launch a Data Hub which could be a tool to generate additional revenue and insight

options.name: Provide Ongoing Support for the Tourism Improvement District (TID)
options.who_is_affected: Tourism/hospitality industry, conventions, and events; the recently legislated TID is an industry-supported funding stream for destination marketing that reduces dependence on annual public budget cycles. Benchmarked to San Diego, Seattle, Denver TIDs.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium-High (role is coordination and support) / Timing Medium (benefits appear over event/convention cycles). Aligning conference incentives with targeted growth sectors and lead-generation.
options.verbatim_anchor: Support ongoing implementation of the TID

options.name: Invest in and Coordinate a Vibrancy Ecosystem
options.who_is_affected: Residents, tourists, and businesses; a coordinated 'vibrancy ecosystem' (waterfront, parks, cultural venues, catalytic entertainment districts) aligns planning, incentives, and public-private partnerships around high-visibility destination assets. Examples cited: waterways strategy, stadium strategy, Museum Campus development, Lakefront improvements.
options.feasibility_note: Impact High / Feasibility Low (capital intensive with complex partnerships) / Timing Long (multi-year development horizon).
options.verbatim_anchor: Invest in a range of destination projects and/or districts

options.name: Ensure Civic Engagement Coordination
options.who_is_affected: Civic, philanthropic, anchor institutions, business leaders, and civic organizations; a formal civic engagement initiative / Office of Civic Partnership aligns philanthropy with City priorities and creates leadership pipelines for emerging leaders. Benchmarked to Indianapolis, Detroit, Pittsburgh partnership models and NYC/LA mayoral funds.
options.feasibility_note: Impact Medium / Feasibility Medium (establishing coordination structure is achievable) / Timing Medium. Illustrative: aligning even a small share of philanthropic capital could represent hundreds of millions annually in additional investment.
options.verbatim_anchor: Establish a formal civic engagement initiative ... Office of Civic Partnership

notes: 58 named recommendations captured across three subcommittees with named menu items: Long-Term Liabilities (10, p.29-37 detail), Revenues & Expenditures (25, p.46-61 detail), Economic Development (23, p.66-84 detail). The Community Insights subcommittee (Section IV, p.14-18) contributes a prioritization/equity framework and survey findings, NOT discrete menu options, so it produced no rows. AMBIGUITIES/JUDGMENT CALLS: (1) This report is overwhelmingly qualitative (Impact/Feasibility/Timing = High/Medium/Low); only two options carry an explicit dollar figure tied to the recommendation itself: LTL-2 CPS contributions ($175M/year for 10 years, p.31) and R&E-5 tax auditors ('up to $56 million in additional annual collections' for a fully staffed Tax Division, plus a $1.0-4.5M/avg $3M per-auditor range, p.49-50) — both captured. (2) Many Economic Development options cite illustrative peer-city or scenario figures (e.g., mHUB $2.0B revenue/7,200 jobs; '$125M' supplier-development scenario; $8.5B receivables; $185B deployed capital) — these are context/benchmarks, NOT the option's own estimate, so dollar_estimate=null with the figures noted in feasibility_note. (3) Program parameters like Missing Middle's '$1 per parcel' and 'up to $150,000 per unit' (p.77) are design parameters, not savings/revenue, left as null. (4) DISSENTS — 18 options carry a dissent. Two are SHARED block-dissents: the library dissent (p.57) applies to all 5 CPL recs (R&E 16-20); the 'Additional Fees, Fines, and Taxes' dissents A/B/C (p.60) apply to all 5 of R&E 21-25, with Dissent C specifically targeting recs 23 (CPI property tax) and 24 (sales-tax expansion). Direction preserved throughout: e.g., LTL-1 and R&E-1 dissents argue the slate does NOT go far enough (add liability reform / progressive taxes), while LTL-4 ADC Dissent A argues 100% funding goes TOO FAR. (5) lever_type for ED growth levers defaulted to 'structural' (no 'economic-development' enum value); 'revenue' used only where the option explicitly creates a revenue stream (Data Hub, Inventory/Monetize Assets) or is a tax/collections measure. (6) timing set to 'recurring' for all 58 — no option is a pure one-time asset sale (the closest, LTL-10, includes ongoing advertising/monetization). (7) Page numbers reference the detailed subcommittee section where the recommendation and its dissent appear, not the Appendix B menu (p.87-92) or per-subcommittee summary tables (p.37, 61, 84). (8) ED section states an 'estimated total implementation cost of approximately $20 million across recommended initiatives' (p.67) — a program-wide cost, not attributable to any single option.
